raw_case_text:
To the Editor: A 24-year-old female nurse was admitted to the emergency room at Bichat University Hospital in Paris, France, on July 4, 2001, with fever, nausea, and general malaise. She had no notable medical history, except spontaneously regressive Schonlein-Henloch purpura at 9 months of age. On admission, after she was given paracetamol, her axillary temperature was 37.6 C. She was slightly jaundiced and reported a mild headache but showed no resistance to head flexion. Her abdomen was depressible but tender. Urinalysis did not show hematuria or signs of urinary infection. Biologic tests indicated normal values except the following: platelets 47.4 x 103/microL, aspartate aminotransferase 307 U/L (normal value <56), alanine aminotransferase 239 U/L (normal value <56), total bilirubin 58 micromol/L (normal value <24), and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 57 U/L (normal value <35). Results of an abdominal echogram were normal. Result of a blood film to identify Plasmodium falciparum was positive for parasitemia at 0.038 per 100 erythrocytes. The patient was given 500 mg of oral quinine three times daily; intravenous quinine was administered 15 hours after admission because she became nauseated. Her malaise persisted for 3 days, but she did not show any signs of malaria. She recovered completely and was discharged on day 6 of hospitalization.
The patient had not traveled outside France except to the United Kingdom years earlier. She did not live near an airport, nor had she been to one recently. She had vacationed in the south of France from June 23 to June 26 but had traveled by car. She had been certified as a registered nurse on May 28 and had been working as a substitute employee at various hospitals in the greater Paris area. On June 21, 2001, she sustained an accidental needlestick injury while taking a blood sample with an 18-gauge, peripheral venous catheter that had no safety feature. She removed the catheter stylet and stuck herself as she crossed her hands to discard the stylet in a sharps container. The needlestick pierced the nurse's glove and caused a deep, blood-letting injury on the anterior aspect of the left wrist. She had no previous history of needlestick injury. She notified the hospital occupational medicine department of her injury on the day it occurred and was given a postexposure interview. In accordance with national postexposure management guidelines, she was tested for HIV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibody, and results were negative at baseline; her immunization against hepatitis B virus (HBV) was confirmed. The risk of infection by pathogens other than HBV, HCV, or HIV following a needlestick injury was not discussed during her postexposure interview, and the nurse was not made aware of that risk. The injured nurse did not inform the managing physician that the injury had occurred while she was drawing blood from a patient to determine if the patient was infected with malaria.
By July 1, 10 days after exposure, fatigue, malaise, and fever developed; her temperature was lowered to 38.6 C by taking paracetamol. Her condition returned to normal on July 2 before a second bout of fever and myalgia occurred during the night. She had to leave work early on July 3 because of generalized pain and a temperature of 39 C. The patient's mother is a biologist and was aware that her daughter had sustained a needlestick injury while drawing blood from a patient in whom malaria was suspected. The mother insisted that a blood smear be performed at a private laboratory in Paris. The smear was qualitatively determined positive for P. vivax. Subsequently, the patient was admitted to Bichat-Claude Bernard University Hospital with suspected malaria. A repeat blood smear conducted there identified P. falciparum.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old female presenting with fever, nausea, headache, and general malaise 10 days after an accidental needlestick injury.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 24-year-old registered nurse sustained an accidental deep needlestick injury to her left wrist with an 18-gauge catheter while drawing blood from a febrile pregnant patient in Paris, France. Ten days post-exposure (July 1), she developed fatigue, malaise, and fever (38.6 C, responsive to paracetamol). Her condition temporarily improved on July 2, but high fever (39 C), myalgias, and generalized pain recurred overnight, forcing her to leave work on July 3. A private laboratory blood smear was reported positive on manual review, prompting admission to a university hospital on July 4.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupational deep, blood-letting needlestick injury on June 21, 2001, to anterior left wrist with a non-safety 18-gauge catheter. No travel outside France except distant childhood travel to the UK; no airport proximity; traveled by car to southern France. Baseline post-exposure testing on injury date: negative for HIV and HCV antibodies, confirmed HBV vaccination immunity. Past medical history: spontaneously regressive Henoch-Schonlein purpura at 9 months of age.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, malaise, nausea, mild headache, and generalized myalgias. Negative for neck stiffness, photophobia, cough, dysuria, or diarrhea. Medications: paracetamol. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Axillary temperature 37.6 C (after paracetamol). Sclerae slightly icteric. Neurological: alert, oriented, mild headache without resistance to neck flexion or meningeal signs. Abdomen: soft, depressible, but tender; no organomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests: platelets 47.4 x 10^3/microL, AST 307 U/L (normal <56), ALT 239 U/L (normal <56), total bilirubin 58 micromol/L (normal <24), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 57 U/L (normal <35). Other routine hematologic and biochemical tests within normal limits. Urinalysis: negative for hematuria or leukocyte esterase. Abdominal ultrasound: normal. Thick and thin peripheral blood films performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Occupationally acquired acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria secondary to accidental needlestick injury, complicated by thrombocytopenia and acute hepatitis/jaundice.
Diagnostic confirmation: Initial private laboratory smear misidentified as P. vivax; repeat reference blood film at Bichat University Hospital definitively identified Plasmodium falciparum with parasitemia of 0.038 per 100 erythrocytes (0.038%).
Treatment & Outcome: Initially treated with oral quinine 500 mg three times daily; switched to intravenous quinine 15 hours after admission due to nausea and vomiting. Malaise persisted for 3 days, followed by rapid clinical and biochemical recovery with normalization of liver transaminases and platelet count, and discharge on hospital day 6.
